notes.meaning: The leaders of the community already lived in Jerusalem, but the newly rebuilt city needed more residents for safety and daily life. The people cast lots—a way of choosing by drawing marked objects to seek God's direction—so that one out of every ten people would move into the holy city while the rest stayed in their home towns. This fair system supplied the capital with the families needed to defend and rebuild it.

Beyond those chosen by lot, some families stepped forward willingly to make their homes in Jerusalem. The community blessed them because moving into the city meant leaving comfortable farms and facing danger from nearby enemies. Their willing sacrifice showed deep love for God's city and the common good of their nation.

Nehemiah introduces a formal record of the provincial leaders who made their homes in Jerusalem. Most of the ordinary Israelites, priests, temple workers, and other families remained in their ancestral towns across the province of Judea. Moving away from their inherited lands often meant exchanging farming livelihoods for difficult city life.

Leaders from the tribe of Judah settled in the capital, led by men like Athaiah and Maaseiah from the family lines of Perez and Shelah. In total, 468 able-bodied men from Perez lived in Jerusalem. These men were known for their strength and courage, making them well suited to defend the city against surrounding hostile neighbors.

A large group from the tribe of Benjamin also moved into Jerusalem, led by Sallu and his relatives Gabbai and Sallai. Their group numbered 928 men, which was larger than the Judah group because Jerusalem historically lay within Benjamin's tribal border. Having these families inside the walls provided a strong guard for the city gates.

Joel son of Zichri served as the chief officer over the Benjaminite residents, acting like a city commander. Judah son of Hassenuah served under him as second-in-command, overseeing the Second District of the city. Having clear leadership helped maintain public order and civilian safety.

Several priestly families took up residence in Jerusalem to lead the worship services at the temple. Seraiah, who came from a leading priestly line, served as the chief official over the house of God. He oversaw the sacred duties and supported the high priest in managing the sanctuary.

More than a thousand priests were assigned to Jerusalem to maintain the daily offerings, sacrifices, and temple care. Adaiah led 242 family heads, while Amashai and his 128 brave associates served under their supervisor Zabdiel. These men were chosen for their practical skill, spiritual devotion, and courage under difficult circumstances.

Members of the tribe of Levi, who were set apart to assist the priests, also made their homes in Jerusalem. Shabbethai and Jozabad were placed in charge of the outside work of the temple, such as repairing the buildings and collecting food and tithes from the surrounding country. Their practical work ensured that the priests had what they needed for daily worship.

Mattaniah, a descendant of the ancient musician Asaph, led the choir and directed the public prayers of thanksgiving during the morning and evening sacrifices. Other Levites like Bakbukiah and Abda assisted him, bringing the total number of Levites living in the holy city to 284. Faithful worship requires both skilled leadership and regular times of praise.

Akkub, Talmon, and their fellow gatekeepers numbered 172 men stationed at the temple gates. Their job was to guard the holy courts, open and shut the entrances, and prevent anything unclean or dangerous from entering. Faithfully watching over God's house protected the entire worshipping community.

The rest of the common people, priests, and Levites lived throughout the towns of Judah on their family landholdings. Meanwhile, the temple servants, who performed basic manual labor for the sanctuary, were placed on the hill of Ophel under leaders named Ziha and Gishpa. Living on this ridge just south of the temple allowed these workers to report quickly for their daily tasks.

Uzzi, a descendant of Asaph, was appointed overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem, particularly guiding the temple musicians. The Persian king had even issued a royal order providing daily rations and pay for these singers so they could focus on their musical duties. This steady support allowed the worship of God to continue with order and joy.

Pethahiah, a member of the tribe of Judah, served as the royal representative between the Persian king and the Jewish people. He handled public administration, heard grievances, and communicated royal policies to the local leaders. Good government depends on honest and accessible bridges between the people and their rulers.

Jewish families from the tribe of Judah repopulated towns and farming villages across their historic territory. These settlements stretched through ancient sites like Kiriath-arba (Hebron), Dibon, Moladah, and down to Beersheba in the far south. Rebuilding these rural communities gave the people land to cultivate and established a stable food supply.

The list of Judahite settlements continues through towns such as Ziklag, En-rimmon, Lachish, and Azekah. Their settlements reached all the way from Beersheba in the southern desert up to the Valley of Hinnom just outside Jerusalem. This broad spread of towns showed how the returning exiles were gradually reoccupying the homeland of their ancestors.

The families from the tribe of Benjamin settled in the territory north of Jerusalem, from Geba to Michmash, Bethel, and Ramah. They also occupied places like Anathoth and Nob, towns famous from earlier Israelite history. Restoring these northern outposts helped secure the approaches to Jerusalem.

Benjaminites also lived in western towns like Hadid, Lod, and Ono, as well as the Valley of the Craftsmen. These towns reached out toward the coastal plain and were known for trade and artisan crafts. God's people made use of both agricultural fields and skilled labor to rebuild their community.

Groups of Levites who were not stationed in Jerusalem were settled among the towns of Judah and Benjamin. Rather than living gathered together in their own cities, they were distributed among the regular population to help teach God's law and assist with worship. God places His servants where their presence can best strengthen others.
